metadata.title: The gendered playing field: Family socioeconomic status and national gender inequality in adolescents’ out-of-school physical activity

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old students from 50 countries/economies, with a final analytic sample of 316,657 after listwise deletion for missing key country-level variables. The manuscript reports weighted descriptive statistics (Table 1) but does not specify the exact PISA student weight variable name or whether complex survey replicate weights were applied in the multilevel negative binomial models. Because the analysis is a multilevel count regression with country-level covariates (GII, GDP per capita, Gini) rather than an ML algorithm, the paper does not discuss ML-specific weight omission; however, the lack of explicit weight-variable reporting prevents confirming whether sampling weights were used for inference. Analysts should, at minimum, use the appropriate PISA student sampling weights and account for the multistage design when reproducing the models, and ensure country-level variables are merged consistently with the weighted estimation framework.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Start from the full PISA 2015 student sample (483,465 adolescents from 73 countries/economies). Restrict to the subset of cases that contain information on adolescents’ out-of-school vigorous physical activity (dependent variable), yielding N=54 countries/economies with PA data. Exclude four additional cases due to missing data on national gender inequality (Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Macau) or neighborhood urbanicity (Sweden), using listwise deletion for missingness on these key country-level variables; final analytic sample is 316,657 students in 50 countries/economies. Supplementary analyses impute the four excluded countries and exclude China to check representativeness; results are reported as stable.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (age 15) out-of-school vigorous physical activity (count of days in past 7 days)
main_findings.target_variable: Out-of-school vigorous physical activity (days per week)
top_predictors: Gender × Family SES × National gender inequality (GII)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel negative binomial regression coefficients (percent-change interpretation): Female vs male −28.8% days (Model 1); SES +8.0% per 1 SD (Model 1); three-way interaction coefficient −0.129 (Model 4) indicating weaker SES moderation under higher GII; dispersion alpha=0.303 (Model 5).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 the study leveraged Gender (female vs male), Family socioeconomic status (ESCS), and National gender inequality (GII)—including the Gender × Family SES and Gender × Family SES × GII interactions—to model out-of-school vigorous physical activity (days per week), finding that female adolescents participate less than male adolescents overall (−28.8%) and that the SES-related reduction in the gender gap is weaker in countries with higher GII (three-way interaction coefficient −0.129). This indicates that policies aiming to reduce gender gaps in adolescent physical activity should target socioeconomic disadvantage more strongly in gender-unequal contexts, because macro-level gender inequality constrains the protective role of family SES.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old adolescents from 50 countries/economies (final N=316,657 after listwise deletion for missing national gender inequality or neighborhood urbanicity). The dependent variable is the self-reported number of days in the past seven days adolescents participated in out-of-school vigorous physical activity, modeled with multilevel negative binomial regression to address overdispersion (alpha≈0.303). Across countries, female adolescents report 28.8% fewer days of out-of-school vigorous PA than male adolescents, while a one–standard deviation increase in family SES is associated with an 8.0% increase in weekly PA. Importantly, the SES moderation of the gender gap diminishes as national gender inequality increases (three-way interaction coefficient about −0.129), and these patterns remain stable after adding controls (in-school PE, math score, school grade, urbanicity, GDP per capita, and Gini). Limitations include reliance on self-reported PA and the absence of explicit survey-weight variable reporting for the inferential models.
